answer: LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding) and node2vec are both network embedding methods, but they use different sampling philosophies. LINE is designed to preserve local network structure in very large information networks by optimizing proximity-based objectives over observed edges and sampled non-edges; in practice, its training uses edge-sampling ideas to scale to large graphs. node2vec, by contrast, learns embeddings from random walks and then applies a skip-gram-style objective to the generated node sequences. The key difference in sampling is that node2vec biases its random walks to interpolate between breadth-first search and depth-first search behavior: BFS-like walks tend to stay near the starting node and capture local neighborhood similarity, while DFS-like walks tend to explore farther nodes and capture more structural equivalence. So, BFS and DFS are not the embedding objectives themselves; they are the two exploration modes that node2vec’s biased walk strategy can emulate, whereas LINE’s sampling is edge-centric rather than walk-centric.
